newsitem.title: USA: Browner stresses no decision yet on air standards.
newsitem.headline: Browner stresses no decision yet on air standards.

text.p: Facing hostile questions from a House panel, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner on Tuesday stressed that her agency had not made a final decision on whether to set tougher air quality standards.
"We are reviewing public comments, and we take that very seriously, and no final decision has been made," Browner told a House appropriations subcommittee.
Panel Chairman Rep. Jerry Lewis, a California Republican, blasted the EPA's proposal to tighten standards against soot and smog, and called it "purely a political policy decision."

"Our panel is concerned that you've already made the decision in your head," Lewis said. "I would guess the folks in the agency feel they are now under the gun to make the science fit the policy. Seems like it's supposed to be the other way around."

The EPA in November proposed setting stricter standards for smog, or ozone pollution, and for soot, or particulate matter pollution. The agency is to announce a final rule by July 19 on smog and soot standards, which industry groups are lobbying to keep at current levels.
Browner has said she will not be swayed from the objective of protecting children's health, but said that did not mean she had decided to set stricter air quality rules.

Lewis said the EPA's admission earlier this month that it over-estimated the number of premature deaths that could be averted by setting new limits on air particle pollution called into question the agency's other analyses.

"If EPA or its contractors and grantees are off by a factor of 25 percent on something as important as the number of premature deaths, how can we ever be sure the rest of the study isn't off by a like amount except by release and public review of all the available data," Lewis said. Browner said the agency was in the process of releasing the data.

The EPA originally said a new standard limiting pollution from tiny air particles that lodge in the lungs would prevent up to 20,000 premature deaths annually, but then revised that estimate to 15,000 after an independent consultant pointed out an error in the agency's conclusions from a scientific study.
